utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everyone. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today is Thursday, the 24th of August. I'd like to say good afternoon to everyone, especially to the person from CMSS who is with us today. And I'd like to thank her for all the things she does for these proceedings to go on smoothly. I'd like to move on to an item related to the hearings and hearings management. I know that the Prosecution is worried about the 24th of October. That is bank holiday, UN bank holiday, and therefore the question arose whether we should have a hearing on the Monday, 23rd of October. We spoke about the matter as Judges, and we believe that we should ask for the position of the Defence, but if the Defence is not opposed to that solution, we could decide not to sits on Monday the 23rd and postpone that hearing to Friday, the 27th, in the morning. In other words, we would have the same amount of hearing time, of sitting time, but the only difference would be that the hearing of Monday would be postponed until Friday. Therefore, if we have a witness who testifies for several days, that witness would not have to wait between Monday and Friday -- and Wednesday. Does the Defence have any objections about that matter? Since there aren't any objections, the Trial Chamber would like to invite the person who is in charge of the hearings and sitting management for us to have a hearing on the 27th in the morning, and I'd like to invite the Prosecution to adapt its witness list in accordance with that new decision. I'm now going to issue two oral rulings, the first one in private session. Mr. Registrar, can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber issues an oral ruling in addition to a previous decision rendered orally by the Trial Chamber. During the hearing of the 21st of August, 2006, the Trial Chamber ruled about the exhibits submitted to the witness on the 17th of August. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, the Trial Chamber would like to specify the numbers of the exhibits it ruled upon on the 21st of August. P 03249; P 08588; P 09413, page 4, 11 and 12; IC 00027; IC 00028; 2D 00083; 2D 00084; 5D 00515. utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and good day to you. utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Valentin Coric wishes to tender the following documents into evidence: 5D 00523, 5D 00534, 5D 00528, 5D 00529, 5D 00524, 5D 00525, 5D 00526, and finally 5D 00527. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar has just told me that there might be a mistake on page 7, line 6 about 3D 00034. It should be 3D 00334.

utterances.text: Sorry. [Interpretation] I have to check this. Your Honour, if you'll give me two minutes to check, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I now call upon the Prosecution to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Have they at least found your baggage at last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's good news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if I may quickly return to two matters yesterday to just correct them. I asked you yesterday whether your youngest child was born in 1993. That was a mistake on my part, I think. Your child born in 1993 was indeed your first child and therefore your oldest child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The second matter that I'd like to clear up, when we spoke about Papak yesterday, is that perhaps the same village as Papci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Papci. Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We concluded yesterday when you said that in June, 1993, you went to Mount Tolovac. Now, just before proceeding on that point, in the time that you stayed in Gracanica, was there any or were there any Muslim armed forces in that immediate area, or Muslim military installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you went to Mount Tolovac in June, 1993, why did you decide to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I decided to go there because it was safer there than in Gracanica. Since it was a mountain, we thought that nobody could get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if you say nobody could get to it, whom did you not want to get to that, or whom did you want to get away from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to escape the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you in a few moments who "we" is that you are referring to, but I'd first like to say -- ask where on Mount Tolovac did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Where on Mount Tolovac did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to a barn that was empty, and we put up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This barn, were there other buildings in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just sheds, five or six, with cattle. People would go up the mountains and that's where they kept their cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your father, is it correct that his cattle was also brought there and kept there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We lived in Gracanica, my mother and sisters and brothers and father, but we took the cattle up there so we could milk the animals and so that my little son would have something to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, your father, you said that he had only one leg. Did he have an artificial leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did have an artificial leg and two crutches. He would put his artificial leg on sometimes, but he couldn't wear it all the time because he had some sores, so he would use his crutches to walk mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you and your family arrived on Mount Tolovac, is it correct that the Munikoza family were already there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were already there. That's where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did any of the people with you on the mountain at that stage wear uniforms, military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did any of you have any weapons, firearms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were bare-handed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were there any military installations in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you gave birth to your son in this cattle stable on the 19th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can move a month on from that moment, around about or on the 18th of July, 1993. Tell us about who came or who arrived at the cattle stable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, Mujo Selimovic came to see where we were and what we were doing. He asked my father whether we were sleeping there. My father said no, we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I could stop you there for a moment. Do you know why Mujo Selimovic came to ask this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that the HVO army paid him and that they had prepared it. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And why are you sure of that? Tell us what happened after his visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from the people that he was paid that they paid him to go and see where they were and what we were doing. I didn't see it myself but I heard it from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On the morning of 19 July, 1993, very early in the morning, tell the Court what happened at this cattle stable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sleeping, and the HVO soldiers arrived at the door. They bashed down the door with their legs. They forced us outside and lined us up and threatened us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At this stage, can you tell us about what time did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At about 2.30 until 4.00 thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And all the people that you had mentioned earlier as being in your group, were all of them still in the cattle stable at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We'd just gone outside because there was nothing that we could have waited for there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was Saban Munikoza still at the stable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Several minutes before that he said he had a strange feeling that the HVO would catch him alive, so he left the house and went off somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers who arrived there, how were they dressed? How did they look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. On their left arms they had the HVO insignia. They had black paint on their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you recognise or did you know which HVO soldiers these were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did know. Milicevic Ivcan and Papak Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps repeat those names just for the record? I didn't hear them clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first person's name was Milicevic, Ivcan Milicevic and Papak Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And these men, do you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that exactly. All I know is that they were from Pavci, the village of Pavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were these the same soldiers whom you had seen or who had frightened you while you were staying in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, they were the same ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you see whether any of these soldiers was in command or issuing orders to the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Papak. He led them. Now, who exactly was that person in command I don't know, but I know that he commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So the soldiers, they ordered you to go outside the barn, and they lined you up or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So what happened then once you were outside the barn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They sent us off to another barn and said they would kill us down there, set fire to us, things like that. They tried to make us afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say "they," are you still referring to the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were frightened. Of course we were frightened because they were armed and we were civilians. We didn't have anything with us, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You were ordered to walk to another barn. Did you walk to this, you and the group, to the other barn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At that stage when you arrived at the other barn, was Bajro Munikoza still with you or with the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't with us. He stayed up there somewhere on the path, and then the HVO soldiers pushed them -- pushed him and hit him with their rifle butts and everything else. I don't know what happened after that, where they took him, but after a few moments we heard the sounds of shooting, gunshots, and I know he never returned to us there on Tolovac mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you see when the soldiers were beating him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw that myself when they pushed and shoved him and hit him with their rifles in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At the second stable, tell us what happened to his wife, Saha Munikoza.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in that second stable I think she asked to go outside, to be allowed to go outside, and they let her go out, and then they took her off somewhere and she never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The people who took her from the stable, did -- was that an HVO soldier or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers, two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And those two soldiers, did they return after having taken Saha away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did return. That's true, they did return. But she wasn't there any more. And when we set off, we found her on -- lying down on the path. I knew she was dead. I was frightened myself when I saw the woman lying down. I'd never seen a dead body before. That was the first time, and I was terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When -- when you saw her body, was this at a stage after the soldiers had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you saw the body of Saha Munikoza, there what did you recognise that as being Saha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw the blood on her back. I assume they shot a bullet at her. I know for certain that it was her, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can return to the events at the barn, can you tell us what happened to your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just have a little rest, please? I feel a little sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam, if we -- if you wish us to take a break, we can do that, or do you want us just to wait a few minutes? How long would you like us to make a break for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten minutes, please, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to adjourn the hearing for 10 minutes, but we'll stay in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Kovacic, during this interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but perhaps this would be a good time to address what you said and the registrar just noted about the error on the transcript, page 7, line 6. The number should read 3D 00334. I apologise for that, and thank you for noticing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. I'd just like to add that because of the emotional state of the witness, I'd like to ask the Prosecution to ask only strictly necessary questions or, rather, the Defence during the cross-examination as well so that we don't upset the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of my own Defence certainly and I think I can speak on behalf of all Defence counsel that nobody will be asking the witness any questions at all. But perhaps I could just say a few words theoretically. The only thing that I could ask was with respect to two documents put forward, P 02294, and P 9401 presented through this witness. I do believe that you've seen the documents, and it would be my proposal that the Prosecution does not tender those documents through this witness. There will be perhaps another opportunity. Do you want me to explain why or shall I cede the floor to my colleague? Perhaps I could just explain. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: according to that list, there are 12 vehicles, and for each of them it stipulates the alleged owner, the type of vehicle, and the date of confiscation. From her previous statement we see that she spent least time in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go back into private session, because we were in open session just then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And this is perhaps in keeping with our discussion that we had yesterday and how to make the process more efficient. There was another ruling in another case by Judge Bonomy from the Bench again. It was on Tuesday, the 22nd of August. The issue hasn't quite come up before us, but in almost every trial it does come up because of the nature of these cases, and that had to do with the Prosecution attempting to introduce additional evidence that they came across through a proofing session, and there was an objection raised by Mr. O'Sullivan, a lawyer who has been around since almost the inception of this institution and a very fine lawyer he is, and he objected often the grounds that it would be unfair to the Defence, and of course Judge Bonomy, being an excellent Judge himself, indicated, well, what do we do when the information that comes in is rather relevant and important? How can you necessarily try to keep it out? And of course the response was that there should be some showing on the part of the Prosecution that they exercise due diligence and despite due diligence this information was unavailable to them. And if it's terribly important, of course, do it through written, if not at least an oral application. In other words, before attempting to introduce this information, this new evidence into court, they should make an application to the Court and make a showing as to why this new information was not available to them in spite of their due diligence. The rule is tangentially connected with Rule 115 when it comes to appeals and I think it's a fair ruling. It's something that Your Honour should keep in mind. I think it's something that you may wish to consider and issue a similar decision. I -- the information is on page 2130, transcript page 2130, starting on line 16, to 2133, transcript of 22nd August, 2006. And I have a copy of it here if the Court wishes, but I'm sure Mr. Registrar will be able to find it quite easily. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the victims of this war when they -- their memories are brought back to what happened to them during the war it's very difficult to examine witnesses like this, but just for the record, I'd like to say that the word "Croatian soldier" or "HVO soldier," keeps being used, that phrase. That implies that he went there in an organised fashion, that he was on assignment following orders. All we know is that we have heard two names and that they were wearing uniforms. When we come to other witnesses, we're going to be able to ask explicit questions to see what they mean when they say the army other soldiers, especially soldiers that were not in barracks, that did not -- that carried their weapons home when they weren't on the battlefield. So they were, in fact, citizens with rifles that they very often bought from their own money. These rifles were procured by themselves. Now, I'm not going to ask that of this witness, of course, but in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's an important point. The Prosecution did not complete its examination-in-chief to determine who those soldiers were, so let's not put the cart before the horse. And I, too, will be asking questions along those lines of the witness. Now, with respect to what Mr. Karnavas just said, you, it appears, have read our thoughts, because this morning we prepared a ruling on precisely the point that you've just raised, and I'd like to assure you that after the break we will be rendering that ruling. We did not know about the Bomomy decision and ruling because each Trial Chamber works completely independently, and we have enough to be getting on with with our own case not to occupy ourselves with other people's cases, but we always tend to keep abreast of what is interesting going on -- what interesting things are going on elsewhere. But your preoccupations will receive a solution from us. It is integrated within the decision or ruling that we're going to give later on which have to do with new elements arising from proofing sessions with the witnesses and how the Prosecution intends to use it. Since we have a few more minutes left before the witness enters, and I have a few more minutes, and I think my colleagues would have said the same thing, do not forget that witness statements are compiled sometimes many years before the witness comes, and as you know, those statements are compiled by the Prosecutor's office, OTP, and so they are -- information is collected in that way. Then several years later when the witness comes into court there's a discussion between the Prosecutor and the witness, and in certain cases the witness can spontaneously recall events that he happens to remember that he forgot to or didn't see the need to tell the investigator about, and then the Prosecutor can -- can question the witness in the interests of justice on that matter. So that is the kind of situation that can arise. And we have taken note of the possibility of such situations arising, and that is why we're going to render a ruling which I hope the Defence will find satisfactory. So you must wait patiently for the ruling to be rendered. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Just one point on the last issue that the Presiding Judge just -- just discussed with respect to the process of proofing and statement-taking. Let me again, for the benefit of everyone so that there's full understanding of some of the -- some of the difficulties inherent in this process, let me also remind Your Honours and my learned colleagues that our statements -- the Office of the Prosecutor takes statements in either English or French, and the witnesses sign those statements based on an oral read-back that they receive at the time those statements are prepared and taken, which as Your Honour rightly points out in some instances is many years ago. Those statements then for purposes of disclosure and other purposes are translated back into B/C/S for the benefit of the Defence and the accused. It is quite often, although not always, but quite often the case that the first time the witness actually sees the statement in their own language is the day before they testify when they are brought here for proofing, and it is quite often at that stage, also many years after the statement was given, that the witness reads the statement in their own language, not only maybe as Your Honour rightly points out, remembers additional items but also has an opportunity to say, "That sentence or at that statement or that paragraph is not quite correct. It needs to be changed." And at that point in time, the investigator or lawyer who are proofing the witness make a note of that and disclose it to the Defence. That disclosure often occurs either the evening before or in some instances, if the proofing went on until late in the evening, the very morning the witness comes into court and testifies. And again, I just wanted to put that out so that everybody understands some of the problems that are inherent in this process where we're dealing in name of different languages and number of years have elapsed in some instances between the time the statement is originally given and the time the witness comes into court to testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- I fully appreciate the process. I'm well aware of it, and we face the same challenges. But this is sort of my first step to the next issue, which is: I don't want them bringing in now new witnesses and adding new witnesses to their case if they see their case perhaps weak here or there, all of sudden they're going out there trying to interview witnesses to bolster their case, because if those witnesses were out there and known to them and they didn't exercise due diligence, don't come crying in and saying, "We need to bring in more witnesses to elongate, to enlarge our case." That's the real purpose behind my -- of this -- of this request. I was just taking -- putting my toe into the water. But the real reason is I want to make sure the Trial Chamber issues a decision that whatever their case is is what's already on their 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. We take good note of what you've said, but experience has taught me here in this case and in other cases that sometimes when a witness answers a question put to him or her by the Prosecution or the Defence, the witness says spontaneously something that is completely new and that is new to everyone in the courtroom. That happens quite often. And sometimes I look at you on both sides and I can see that you are surprised, nobody was expecting such a response from the witness. And then quite logically, for the Prosecution or the Defence, this new piece of information, this new piece of evidence will require additional questioning, additional investigation maybe. And that might explain what you regret, is that sometimes new witnesses are requested or put on the list. But that's the way the judicial process goes. But even in civil law countries it happens that you have witnesses who come to testify it and who reveal new developments, new information at the last minute, and then you have to call additional witnesses, whereas the trial has already started. These things happen. Very well. We've just been told that the witness is now in a position to resume the testimony. We'll pull the blinds down and have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back into open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm sorry that I have to put you or have to cause you to relive these moments, and I truly do understand your grief. Could you tell us, just before we proceed, how many men there were, approximately, on Mount Tolovac that evening with HVO uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 15 HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what happened to your father that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in that stable. They made us come out, and then my father started releasing the cattle from one stable to the next. I asked the soldiers to let me go and fetch some extra clothing for my son. They told me I could go. I set out with him. In the meantime, my father wanted to take some bread for my child from one of the stables and asked for permission to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I may -- if may intervene. I'm a bit confused, because I thought that on that day you were giving birth to your first child. Maybe there was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a month afterwards when my father was killed. My son was born on the 19th of June, and my father was killed on the 19th of July, precisely a month later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, sorry for interrupting. You've just stated that you were allowed to give bread to your -- to your child, but when a child is one month old, he doesn't eat bread.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was referring to my sister- in-law's son. She stayed behind in the stable. It was my sister-in-law's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Thank you for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, the -- when you and your father -- when you went with your father when he released the cattle, was this going back to the very first stable where the events had started that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we went back, right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the other people in your group, did they remain at the second stable where you had been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They remained at the second stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So in this first stable, your father, he then wanted to find some bread. Tell us what happened then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what happened was a soldier said to him, "There's no salvation for you any more." I was pushed out by two HVO soldiers. They killed him. They fired a whole round into him. In the meantime, they poured some liquid over him and set him on fire. When the two men left, I saw the fire spreading to the whole stable. There was nothing I could do. I was weeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The soldiers, they left you at the stable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They left me there. They went off, and I stayed there. I left all the things I had taken. I didn't have the strength to pick them up and carry them away. I had no change of clothing for my child. My child was always wet and hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- do you know which soldier shot your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do. The two of them were Ivica Papak and Ivcan Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. After this happened and when the soldiers had left, is it correct that your family was also left and they fled into the forest, or they hid in the forest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did hide in the forest. I found my sister crying on the road. I asked her what was going on. She was frightened. I have no words to describe it. I know how we felt and what had happened to us up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you and your family, is it correct that you then went to the hamlet of Paros, which is a little distance away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We went there. We found refuge with an elderly woman. We stayed there for two or three days. After that, two HVO soldiers arrived and asked us to surrender. I decided there was nothing I could do but surrender. My child was always hungry. So were all us, but I cared most about my son. I had nothing to feed him with. I convinced my mother and my sisters that we should all go, that we should all surrender. I was the first to surrender, and then they all followed me, and that's how we came to Crni Most, the black bridge. A bus came along and picked us up. We arrived in Prozor, in Podgradze, a small village mostly inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The menfolk in your group, well,your husband, I think, did he accompany you or did he go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they went to the forest. They were hiding in the woods. Think didn't want to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if you say surrender, what do you mean by surrender? To whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We surrender to the HVO. We had to give ourselves up. We had no choice but to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was it possible for you to instead go to territory under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't possible. It was all cut off. It was all held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In Podgradze when you and your family arrived there, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found an abandoned house where we moved in. We asked the woman to give us the house keys. The man who owned the house and his wife were somewhere in Germany. This woman gave us the key. There were about 90 of us there. I stayed there with my son. There was nowhere to put him down. I had no change of clothes for him, no food. I had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just to place this in time, was this during the last week of July, 1993, that you moved into this house in Podgradze?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. No, I didn't. The main reason I surrendered was that none of us had anything to eat. But I didn't feel good about it. I had had to surrender. My parents, myself, my sisters, my sister-in-law, we were all there. We had to give ourselves up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you threatened in any way while living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers came along and threatened us. They took away girls and young women. They raped them. I heard about this, but I didn't see

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar will now issue an order to remove the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, if we could perhaps go into private session for a moment to deal with this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, without mentioning the name, what was it that you heard about this girl, what had happened to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from the people in that house that she was taken to the firefighters' home and raped. Soldiers would come to get her. She was the one most often arrested and taken to Prozor and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You and your sisters and your sister-in-law, none of you were raped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank God, no. As soon as night fell, we would go into the woods and spend the night there. And there was someone always watching, awake, to make sure that no HVO men arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you stayed in this house for a few weeks until around the end of August, 1993. Could you tell the Court how it came that you left Podgradze?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite simply HVO soldiers came up to us and said, "You have five minutes to pack up and get out." They said trucks would arrive to take us away. We were glad to be leaving, wherever they would take us. In the meantime, we went to the village of Kucani where they unloaded us, and then they escorted us a little way, and then they started shooting. I know a woman from Lapsunj Prozor was killed there. I know they killed her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The people that you -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Are you okay? Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you say you went to Kucani, were you taken there by truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- by truck. We were taken there by truck. There were trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if you refer to "we," is that the 6.000 people you were referring to who were staying in Prozor and Podgradze?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six thousand Muslims were expelled in that night, women, children, some elderly men, but there weren't many of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if you say expelled from Celina, where did you go to? Sorry, my mistake. If I could correct that. Is it correct that you walked towards Celina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what is the distance between Kucani and Celina, if you could give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely. About three or four kilometres, but I'm not sure. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Celina, is that in territory held by the ABiH at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, shortly or a while after arriving in Celina, is it correct that you and your husband returned to Dreznica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's true. It's correct. We went across one night, and the next day my husband came through the woods, but I couldn't recognise him when I saw him. He was all dirty. He had a beard. I remember that well. It looked as if he hadn't had a bath for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your mother, was she able to return to Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when, but she was brought back. The international community helped. A house was built. My brother and sisters and mother live there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What had happened to the opened house that you stayed in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was burnt to the ground. Nothing was left. Everything of use was taken away and what was left was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about the other houses in Gracanica? Were they also burnt in a similar way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of them. Some have been repaired and some have still not been rebuilt. Three or four houses have not been rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it correct you don't know specifically when the houses were burnt or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall. My head is so full of all this. I can't remember everything any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I would, in conclusion, like to deal with you with two documents, Your Honour, but this may be -- I see the time. It is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's better to have the break now in order to allow the witness to have a rest. It's a quarter to 4.00. We'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, and we'll stay in open session until we resume the testimony of the witness, because as I have announced it earlier on, the Trial Chamber is going to issue two rulings. The first one rendered orally has to do with Witness Tomljanovich from the Prosecution. The Chamber has received an oral motion from the accused Cosic dated 23rd of August, 2006. The accused Cosic through his lawyer Mr. Murphy, would request -- requests the Trial Chamber to reconsider its oral decision rendered on the 26th of June, 2006, that grants expert status to Witness Tomljanovich. His motion is found on an order or a decision rendered in the Milutinovic case on the 13th of July about the expert status of a staff member of the Office of the Prosecutor. The Trial Chamber would like to recall that it has already ruled on the expert status of Witness Tomljanovich based on the inspection of his expert report, his CV, and that the Chamber has also taken into account the fact that the witness is a staff member of the Office of the Prosecutor. As a result, the Trial Chamber has no reason and sees no reason to reconsider its previous decision. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber would like to recall that the Defence, during the cross-examination of the witness, will be in a position to challenge the credibility of the witness as well as the expert report submitted by the witness. Second oral ruling. This is only the fourth decision rendered orally today. This is a ruling modifying the decision of the 3rd of July, 2006. During the hearing of the 23rd of August, 2006, the Accused Prlic stated that during the examination of the witnesses the Prosecution covers issues that have not been the summaries prepared in accordance with Rule 65 ter. The Chamber would like to refer the parties to its oral decision of the 3rd of July, 2006, pages 42 to 48 and 48 to 49. In its decision, the Trial Chamber decided as follows, and I quote: "The Prosecutor, as far as possible, shall limit the examination of witness to the issues mentioned in the summaries prepared in accordance with Rule 65 ter." The Chamber had admitted that, and I quote again: "The Prosecutor might expand the examination to issues not mentioned in the summaries, but issues that would have been raised during the proofing session of the witnesses, but this provided for that the Defence be notified as quickly as possible through any technical means available in order to allow the Defence to prepare itself properly for the cross- examination of the witness." Let me now tell you what's new in this decision with respect to the previous decision. Considering that the Chamber has to make sure that the rights of the accused are complied with, that the accused are in a position to prepare their cross-examinations properly, the Trial Chamber hereby decides today, and I would like to ask the Prosecution to listen very carefully, the Prosecution has to disclose to the legal officers of the Chamber any new information based or due to the proofing of a witness and this at the same time, at the same time, as this same information is being disclosed to the Defence. This will allow the Chamber to rule knowingly about any possible objections raised by the Defence with regard to these new matters. So to sum up, if, during the proofing session, the Prosecution finds out that there are new items arising, new evidence that is going to be raised during the examination of the witness, then the Prosecution has to inform the Defence - that's always been the case - but the Prosecution also has the obligation to notify the legal officer of the Trial Chamber, and thus the legal officer will be informed, let's say, at 3.00 a.m. by e- mail that such-and-such item will be raised and it's new, and thereafter the Judges will be informed of the same and we will then be in a position to consider the matter and rule on any objections. So if we compare this to the decision of the 3rd July, 2006, we've streamlined this previous decision, including this scheme, this mechanism that should be satisfactory to everyone. And this is once again in the interest of justice here. I have spent a few minutes on these decisions, but now I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps just one issue for purposes of clarification would be very helpful to the Prosecution in order to comply with this order. Perhaps we could be informed in advance of which legal officer is responsible for which witness or to whom we are to provide this information as there are a number of legal officers assigned to this case, so as to avoid confusion or perhaps us informing a legal officer who happens to be on leave on that day. If there is duty roster or if you want to sent to the same legal officer or all of them or which ones, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. So theoretically speaking or practically speaking, the legal officer are P4 staff member, P3 staff member plus their assistants but you know all of them, of course. The main actor here is Tatjana Maikowski, the Trial Chamber's legal officer who is available 24/7. She is your privilege "intelliputer," and if she's not available, and that can happen, of course then you can get in touch with the other assistants that will replace her. So in other words, there is always someone available. So for any reason she's not available, then she has to make sure that the lines of communication remain open with someone else. So don't about worry. The Judges shall be informed without any problem. I hope I have put your mind at rest, Mr. Mundis. Up until now, things have worked fine. So far the communication has been fine. Sometimes there are hiccups in communication but until now things have been going smoothly. And you have to think that I'm very often here at the Tribunal as early as 6.00 a.m., so if need be you can always try to get in touch with me. And my assistants have mobile phones that are always accessible, so you can always get in touch with them. Don't forget the computer systems here at the Tribunal, the e-mail system whereby you can disclose the necessary information. Witness, please accept our apologies. We had to deal with matters of procedure because the Defence was expecting our decisions. Now I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, a few final things, then. You have referred a number of times during your evidence to Ivica Papak as being one of the soldiers. Is this his real name or is this a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't say really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about somebody else. Do you know an Ivan Tomic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Ivica Papak, where did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, I do know Ivica Papak. I apologise. I do know Ivica Papak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where do you know Ivica Papak from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've known him since childhood. He went to school in Gracanica. I know him very well. He would come to my house countless time when we were children. We would even go to school together in Gracanica because there was no school in Papci but in Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Papak, was that his surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your father, his body was never recovered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It was never found. And I would like to find it so that I can go to his grave and put some flowers on his grave just like everybody else, to put flowers of the grave of my nearest and dearest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session for purposes of dealing with the first document I wish to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you a final document which is similar to the one you have just seen, and that is Exhibit 8608. I don't know whether it would be easier to once again show the hard-copy version on the ELMO. Yes. Thank you. That is the correct document? Witness, this is a similar document than the previous one you've seen, and it is also an extract from the register of deaths, and it's page 64. Do you see that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And do you see that the first certificate relates to Bajro Munikoza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in regard to this, it says that the day, month, and year of death, that's just above where you see his name, was 29 July, 1993, and it was at Skrobucani. According to your information, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is correct, because he was taken off certainly. I heard about that. I didn't see it, but I heard he was taken to Skrobucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is this the same Bajro Munikoza that you had testified about earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it is, yes. It couldn't be anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we move down to the second half of the document. This certificate or extract from the death register relates to Saha Munikoza. Is that the same, to your knowledge, Saha whom you testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: With regard to her, it says that she died on 29 July, 1993. To your knowledge, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, it's not correct. Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When did she die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she died on the 19th of July, the same day when my father was killed. That same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And when it says Skrobucani, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Skrobucani is right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And why would you say that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's five minutes' difference. What did you say? Correct. Skrobucani is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about Tolovac? Is Skrobucani and Tolovac, are they close by or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add a question? You said that the date of 29th July for the death of Bajro Munikoza was probably correct. Earlier today, you have told us that on the 19th July, they took him away, and then you heard a number of shots.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's right. That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So would you agree that perhaps this date is also wrong, as is the other date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it is wrong. I've just noticed that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes the examination-in-chief of the Prosecution. The Judges have a number of questions to ask about the persons who killed your father, and my colleague wants to ask a question first, and I will be asking some questions to complete his afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, I would like some clarification on who the assassins of your father were, who perpetrated the act. You said that on the 19th of July, two soldiers of the HVO, and you gave us their names, you said that. Now, my first question: You said that you knew those soldiers, that you went to the same school together; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So probably those soldiers were from your village or the neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, near my village. About half an hour away. Their village was half an hour away from mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, you said that they belonged to the HVO. How could you know that those soldiers were HVO soldiers? Can you tell us what you base that on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they -- on their left arm they had the HVO patches, and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war, did those soldiers stay in the area or did they go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. I don't know, because I went to Dreznica. So I can't say whether they stayed there or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more question, madam. Do you know if there were any court proceedings against those soldiers with respect to those criminal acts that they perpetrated or with respect to other criminal acts that they might have perpetrated? Were these two soldiers prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't say. I don't really know, because as I said, I went to Dreznica. I left, so I don't know anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam, I also have a series of questions to ask you about those HVO soldiers, and we've come to the heart of the matter now, because the Judges have to make decisions. Now, you told us that there were 15, approximately 15 of them, I suppose, and that according to you, they seemed to be under the command of the person you went to school with, and his first name was Ivica. Now, the 15 soldiers, 15 HVO soldiers, were they all wearing -- dressed in the same way, wearing the same clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were all wearing HVO uniforms, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, since you were an eyewitness, you were there yourself, in your recollections this group, did you feel that they were an organised group? Did they give the impression of being an organised group commanded by your ex-fellow classmate, or do you remember them as being a disparate group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what it was like. They stormed the house quickly. I didn't know what was going on. That's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said on their left arm they had the HVO insignia. In your recollection were there other signs, other insignias they were wearing or was this the only insignia you could see on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please describe us how -- what they were wearing? They had trousers, a jacket, a hat. You gave a very specific piece of information. You said they had markings on their faces, their faces painted. But apart from this, if you think back of that time, can you -- what can you tell us about their clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only remember they had jackets, trousers, shirts. That's all I remember. I can't remember anything else. They had boots on their feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as their weapons are concerned, you're probably not a specialist in the matter, but as far as you can recollect, did -- was each one of them carrying a weapon? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. They all had rifles. I don't know what the names of the rifles are. I'd seen them for the first time. All I know is that they all carried rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me the following question, because this is very important for us Judges. Please allow me to go back to this very painful moment you had to go through. According to what you've told us, it seems that one of the soldiers spoke to your father before shooting him. What about the other soldiers? Were they around them, or were there only one or two soldiers there, one or two soldiers who shot on your father, who opened fire on your father, or were all the soldiers present when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were only two soldiers there. The others were standing around the stable as if they were standing guard. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on throughout these years, did you ever wonder why your father was killed by these two soldiers? Why not you? Why did they choose to kill your father? Did you manage to find an explanation or an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing I can say. Quite simply, I don't know why he was killed. He didn't hurt anyone. He was an invalid. He couldn't go anywhere. He couldn't walk properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the following years, putting aside the interviews you had with the Office of the Prosecutor, you did not report this crime to the judicial authorities in your region, did you? I'm talking about you personally or any other member of your family. Did anyone in your family circle go to the police to report what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't myself, but my mother did. She wanted his body to be found and buried properly, but nothing has been found yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying that your mother tried to do something about it, but unfortunately that -- this was to no avail because the body of your father was never recovered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the village where you lived, you told us that in that village the majority of the population was Muslim. Throughout that period, throughout the period before the 19th of July, during the month of May and during the month of June, the HVO, as you see it, was this HVO -- was the HVO army present in the area? Did you know whether the HVO was around there or the ABiH? In other words, did you know if -- there were military personnel or soldiers in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers there, but I don't know what soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were aware that there were soldiers in the area, and you're telling us that on the 19th of July, you could tell they were from the HVO because you had a look at their patches.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination of the witness, but my fellow Judges might have additional questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was more than one vehicle. There was soldiers from Jajce who did nothing to us, didn't mistreat anyone. I know that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you know how many vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't tell you precisely how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And can you describe any of the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't accept that I know they had camouflage colours on them, like leaves. They were mostly trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I suppose you did not pay any attention to the licence plates, or did you per chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can understand that. It was dark anyway, at least when they arrived, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did they in some way illuminate the scene, for instance, by the headlights of the cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't. I don't know. I don't know that they did, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now, we have two more incidents at least where you mentioned soldiers. One is when you were picked up. I think it was in Crni Most. Those soldiers, I think -- you said that they were from HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you also recognised them by the insignia on the arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you say whether these were soldiers that had also been involved on the 19th of July, or were they knew to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember all the details any more. I don't know any more. But I know there was Ivica from Rumboci. I don't know his last name. He had a red Golf, I know that. But I don't know his last name now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber how many soldiers had turned up on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. It's not all in my head any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand this. Was it two or was it a bigger group? Can you say that much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There -- it was a bigger group, but I can't tell you exactly how many there were, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's already a good answer. Thank you. You were then taken away in a vehicle from Crni Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a bus. There was a bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Bus. Did you by any chance -- have you any memory of the licence plates of that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I would then like to go one step on to the time when you were held in Podgradze, I think it was. There you described to us that HVO soldiers picked up girls and young women and took them away, and they were then sexually abused. Who were those soldiers? What did they look like? Were there any that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know any of them, but I do know they were HVO soldiers and that they took away girls and young women. I know that. As soon as night fell, they would burst into the house and take away whoever they could catch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You had witnessed other engagements of these -- of HVO soldiers. You have told us that on the 19th of July they seemed to be organised. Did you have the impression that when they stormed the houses, as you just said, they were also in some way organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Were they by any chance drunk, mostly, or sometimes, or never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly. Mostly they were drunk, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And did they mostly come during the day or did they come at a time when you had the impression it was their time off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't come by day. Mostly when night fell. That's when they would come and burst in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. An additional question following to an answer you've given to my fellow Judge. These young ladies who were taken away by these drunken soldiers and then abused sexually, later on, did you talk to some of them? Did you ever talk to a young lady who was taken away by the soldiers who then told you about what happened to her, or did you -- or do you know about this because you were told about it by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard it. But who told you about it, the victims themselves or other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it from the women who were abused and raped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, what you are stating now, is that these women who were raped told you about it later on, told you about it yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would talk in the room while we all slept, so I heard them talking about it. They told all of us what had happened. They didn't say that just to me but to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you heard it yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it with my own ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may go on on the same problem. You were in that house for about a month, if I'm -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now, did this taking away of girls and young women occur one, two, or three times, or did it occur almost every night? Can you tell us something about the frequency of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't be precise now, but in a week it would be once or twice at least. I can't tell you exactly how many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Now I'm going to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will look at my colleagues first to see if they object to my starting. It's not my turn, but I'll be very brief, but Your Honour happened to look at me and I happened to have questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will first introduce myself, Witness. My name is Senka Nozica, and I am the Defence counsel of Mr. Bruno Stojic. Please, my first question to you is: Did you make any statements to any investigating organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina about the events you have described here in the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness document -- it's a record, and it contains her statement before the agency for investigation and documentation in Mostar in 1997. I haven't prepared it for e-court. I don't know whether I will tender it, but it's a Prosecution document given to us. Could the witness look at it, please, and then please put it on the ELMO. Put the front page on the ELMO. Can the witness take a look at the signature. Your Honours, do we have to go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do. Mr. Registrar, you have been kept very busy, but we have to go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All I want to do is confirm that in 1997 when you gave the statement to the Agency for Investigation and Documentation, the Mostar sector, made no mention of the fact that anybody disturbed you at night. You said that nobody touched you, and then you said, "Six months later we were expelled to Buturovic Polje." Is that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I just have two more questions for you. How do you know that at that point, 6.000 people started out towards Buturovic Polje? I'm asking you, because based on all the statements that we were provided by the Prosecution, we never heard of that figure. Did you know that personally, or did somebody tell you that later, that in the column there was 6.000 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's true there were 6.000 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know that on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew it from before, because we were all there, all Muslims there in the village of Podgradze. We were all put up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the village of Podgradze, as you say, there were 6.000 people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you all set out together on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, link to the detail when you said, "We surrendered" or "Gave ourselves up to the HVO," the bus, it's the detail when you say you got into the bus, did I hear you correctly, did you say you stopped the bus and it took you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said you hitchhiked the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I insist -- I am insisting on that, because Judge Trechsel asked whether you were taken up, so I wanted to clarify that point. But I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Counsel Alaburic, counsel has just raised the matter of a statement that you made where you made no mention of the fact that some women were, at night, the object of soldiers' attentions. Now, why didn't you say that in 1997 when you told us this a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say so because I had a sick son. He had a brain inflammation. My child was in hospital in Sarajevo all the time. So that's why. And when I went back from Sarajevo, my other son became ill too. There was something wrong with his stomach. So that's why. I can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: When you were shown the statement given by you, signed by you some time ago in 1997 in Mostar, you said you could not remember. In the meantime, did the memory come back? Do you remember that you made such a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the statement I gave, but I can't remember. My son was ill. My husband was ill. I seemed to have got the worst part of life to deal with. My husband was operated on twice. He's a diabetic. I have seven children. I just can't remember anything. It just won't fit into my head any more. So I have to -- the -- all my family relies on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have all my sympathy, madam. Still, do you perhaps remember whether you went to Mostar on your own initiative or whether you were called to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they called me to go there and I went, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I would have liked to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, my name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb and I'm here as Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic. I apologise for having to ask you some questions, but I consider that it is our duty to try and clarify certain points, and that's what I'm going to do. I'd like to ask the usher, please, to put that same statement of the witness on the ELMO, and I'd also like to ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Valentin Coric has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to interrupt, but Mr. President and Your Honours, the Prosecution would object to the accused or any of the accused cross-examining crime base witnesses such as the current witness. The Trial Chamber's revised guidelines from 26 -- or 28 April are very clear that when these -- because these accused are represented by counsel, that the accused may put questions to witnesses only in exceptional circumstances, whereas perhaps due to certain witness's testimony concerning technical matters or technical military matters there might be exceptional circumstances, the Prosecution believes it's inappropriate for any of the accused to be cross-examining crime base witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that if Mr. Praljak is on his feet, that's because he wants to ask technical questions to the witness about the HVO soldiers, and that's at the heart of the case. I suppose, Mr. Kovacic, that what your client intends to do is to deal only with technical issues about the units these soldiers belonged to, an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to my conversation with my client, the question would be yes, but I wish to respond to what my learned friend has said. I feel that these circumstances are exceptional and that his special knowledge is required. He will explain what the special circumstances are, why he feels he needs to put questions, and Your Honours will decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you, yourself, you're not in a position to ask these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the way my client wants to puts the questions, because he was there, I feel that his approach is different. You will hear his arguments, and he is prepared to face the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you say that he was there. He was not there on the spot. Where was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but he was in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in the area. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, why can't you put these questions to the witness through your counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
